hints: Focus on where all the carbon in the carbon dioxide must have come from, it can only come from the hydrocarbon Q.
Start by converting 3.22 g of $\text{CO}_2$ into moles, then into mass of carbon present in the original 1.00 g sample.
Work out the percentage by mass of carbon in Q, then check which listed hydrocarbon has that same carbon percentage from its formula.
walkthrough:
**Find moles of carbon from the CO2**

All the carbon in Q ends up as $\text{CO}_2$. So moles of C in Q equals moles of $\text{CO}_2$ made.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$n(\text{CO}_2) = \frac{m}{M_r} = \frac{3.22}{44.0} = 0.0732 \text{ mol}$$

**Find the percentage of carbon in Q**

Each mole of carbon has mass 12.0 g, so we can find the mass of carbon in the 1.00 g sample.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$m(\text{C}) = 0.0732 \times 12.0 = 0.878 \text{ g}$$
$$\% \text{C in Q} = \frac{0.878}{1.00} \times 100 = 87.8\%$$

**Match this to a hydrocarbon formula**

For any hydrocarbon $\text{C}_x\text{H}_y$, $\%\text{C} = 12x / M_r \times 100$. Only one option gives about 87.8%.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{cyclohexene, C}_6\text{H}_{10}: M_r = 82.0, \%\text{C} = \frac{72.0}{82.0} \times 100 = 87.8\%$$

options.A: Cyclohexene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$ with $M_r = 82.0$. Its carbon percentage is (72.0/82.0) x 100 = 87.8%, which exactly matches the 87.8% found from the combustion data. So 1.00 g gives 3.22 g of $\text{CO}_2$.
options.B: Cyclopentane is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ with $M_r = 70.0$. Its carbon percentage is (60.0/70.0) x 100 = 85.7%, which is too low. It would give only about 3.14 g of $\text{CO}_2$ from 1.00 g.
options.C: Ethene is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ with $M_r = 28.0$. Its carbon percentage is also (24.0/28.0) x 100 = 85.7%, the same empirical ratio as cyclopentane. This is a common trap if you only think about alkenes in general.
options.D: Pentane is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$ with $M_r = 72.0$. Its carbon percentage is (60.0/72.0) x 100 = 83.3%, which is the lowest of the four because alkanes have the most hydrogen. It would give only about 3.06 g of $\text{CO}_2$.
